As someone who does repair their own appliances, it's not as easy as this guy makes it sound.

I've invested quite a bit of money over the years into tools, some rather specialized. Gone are the days that all you needed was a wrench and some elbow grease and you could fix anything.

My blender broke recently; there was a fault in the micro-controller on it and after doing some Googling was able to find the schematics and replicate it's basic function. I lost the on screen display and the built in recipes, etc.... but it'll run when I push a button now.

I ended up having to use everything from my oscilloscope to determine the fault, to software to design the replacement circuit, to my UV lamp and chemical baths to etch the board, and lastly my drill press to drill it and then solder on components.

I once had an LCD monitor conk out on me and with a bit of googling and a few upgraded capacitors from an electronic supply wholesaler I was able to not only repair it, but make it better. I agree that there are certain things a person should be willing to learn how to do themselves, but you find very quickly that knowing how to do it doesn't mean it needs to be done regularly and then you're left with a time vacuum while you're waiting for useful things to do. At that point, it's fair game for hobbies, no explanation or justification required.
